To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the security of postquantum KEM-based key exchanges can be improved by using a split KEM framework, but that the framework is currently not strong enough to provide the desired properties.

(1) we propose the notion of split KEM to enable the translation of DH-based protocols to KEM-based ones and (2) we show that this notion can be used to lift X3DH to a post-quantum key exchange protocol.

(i) we introduce the notion split KEMs, (ii) we show that split KEMs are necessary for the design of post-quantum key exchange protocols, and (iii) we show that it is challenging to instantiate split KEMs in a post-quantum way.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following question: Can we design a post-quantum key exchange protocol that can replace DH-based ones in a protocol flow, while retaining the same properties?
the question: “What would a post-quantum X3DH look like?”.
the question of whether we can design post-quantum key exchange protocols that are as efficient and versatile as the ones based on the Diffi–Hellman primitive.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
we are not yet there.
we do not know how to do it yet.
the question of how to design post-quantum key exchanges that are secure under key reuse remains open.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, in the post-quantume era, we will have to give up the DH primitive as a whole and not only its quantum-secure instantiation.
we show that the post-quantumsafe key-exchange problem is not as simple as one may expect.
we are able to prove that the Signal protocol can be securely instantiated in the post-quantume setting, but we are not able to prove the same for the underlying KEM.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the design of post-quantum key exchanges is a much more challenging task than it seems at first glance.
the post-quantumsafe DH primitive is not just about replacing the underlying algebraic structure but also requires a protocol-level redesign.
post-quantum key exchanges based on KEMs need to be treated differently compared to their classical counterparts.
